notDoing.title: Four things you won’t find here.
notDoing.subtitle: Worth saying before you ask, because the industry is full of all four.

items.title: Accessibility overlays and widgets
items.description: That floating button promising to fix everything with one line of script. It doesn’t touch the code, it hides the problem, and in the United States there are lawsuits against sites that had one installed. If you have one, I’ll tell you to remove it.

items.title: Conformance seals and certificates
items.description: Neither Law 11/2023 nor RD 1112/2018 provides for an official seal that anyone can issue you. What does exist is the accessibility statement or information that you publish and that you answer for. That I do deliver, written and ready.

items.title: Open-ended retainers with no scope
items.description: A monthly fee nobody can define ends up being a monthly fee that covers nothing. Everything on this page has a written scope and a fixed price before we start.

items.title: Automated-only audits
items.description: Tools find some of the problems, never all of them: they catch contrast, but not focus getting lost halfway through your form, nor a screen reader announcing your buy button as “empty link”. That only shows up navigating by hand. An axe report exported to PDF is not an audit.

items.question: How does billing work?
items.answer: 50% on confirmation and 50% on delivery. Formal invoice with VAT, valid for deduction. Ongoing compliance is billed monthly in arrears. The express diagnosis is the exception: it is paid in full up front, in a single payment.

items.question: What is the difference between the express diagnosis and the audit?
items.answer: Depth, and what you take away. The diagnosis walks your homepage and up to three journeys along their main path and gives you the 10 findings costing you most: it answers "do I have a problem, and how big?". The audit evaluates the 55 WCAG 2.2 AA criteria over a documented sample, audits every complete process including its error states, and delivers the remediation plan and the compliance document the law requires: it answers "what am I missing, and how do I close it?". That is why one costs €290 and the other from €1,200.

items.question: Can I book remediation without the audit?
items.answer: If you bring me a recent and sufficiently detailed accessibility report, yes. If you don’t have one, the audit is the prior step: you can’t seriously fix what hasn’t been diagnosed.

items.question: How do I know which tier my site falls into?
items.answer: By what people can do on it. If it only informs and receives enquiries, Essential. If people can buy, book or request an appointment, Commercial. If there are several of those processes or a private area with login, a fixed quote within 24 hours. I verify the size in your sitemap — you don’t have to count pages.

items.question: Do you work with my in-house team or my agency?
items.answer: Yes, and that’s the most common setup. The report is written so any technical profile can act on it directly. If you’d rather they apply it, that’s fine: I audit, and then I review the result.

items.question: What if you miss a finding?
items.answer: It depends on the service. In the audit: if a finding within the audited scope slips past me, I document it and correct the report at no cost within 60 days of delivery. In remediation: if a fix fails the test it was verified with, I redo it at no cost within that same period. The express diagnosis does not carry this guarantee: by design it is a top 10, not a complete evaluation; what I do guarantee is that every finding is confirmed and reproducible.

concerns.label: What worries you
concerns.title: What people ask me before we start.
concerns.intro: Nobody writes to me to talk about WebGL. They write because their site is slow, looks odd on mobile, doesn’t show up on Google, or they’ve heard about the accessibility law. These are the answers.

items.question: Will it be fast?
items.answer: On your customer’s mid-range phone, which is where it counts, not on the computer it was designed on. I load only what each moment needs and I measure it before handing it over.

items.question: Will it look right on mobile?
items.answer: It’s designed for mobile first and tested at 320 pixels wide, in landscape and with text enlarged to 400%. If something doesn’t fit, it’s rearranged. Not hidden.

items.question: Can anyone use it? Does it meet the law?
items.answer: I work to WCAG 2.2 AA, which covers everything the law requires today and what the next version of the European standard will require. And I check it by hand: keyboard, measured contrast and a real screen reader. I audited this very site that way.

items.question: Will Google find it?
items.answer: Google reads text, not images or 3D scenes. So everything that matters goes in HTML, with proper titles, descriptions and a clear structure, even with 3D on top. I won’t promise you the top spot: nobody serious can. What I can make sure of is that Google can read and understand everything you offer.

items.question: How much does it cost?
items.answer: You get a fixed price before we start. For accessibility, the rates are published. In 3D no two projects are alike, so first we talk about what you need to show and I send you a fixed quote, with no surprises later.

items.question: Who will I be talking to?
items.answer: Me, from start to finish. I design it, build it and test it. No salesperson selling you one thing while a team somewhere else understands another.

difference.label: Your questions
difference.title: Making it pretty is the easy part.
difference.subtitle: A 3D experience impresses for the first ten seconds. Whether it sells depends on the rest: that it loads on a mid-range phone, that Google finds it, that it works without a mouse and that it doesn’t make anyone dizzy. Every answer comes with a live proof.

items.title: Won’t it be slow on mobile?
items.description: Not if it’s built for mobile from the start: geometry and textures at just the right size, and the screen only repaints when something changes. In VETA, all 48 surfaces are drawn in a single call to the graphics card.

items.title: Will Google find it?
items.description: Google doesn’t look inside a 3D scene: it reads text. So everything that matters (names, descriptions, product sheets) also lives in HTML, with its own title and description for search engines. The 3D sits on top of the text, not in place of it.

items.title: What about people who don’t use a mouse?
items.description: Arrows, Enter and Escape do what you expect. The mouse is an option, not a requirement.

items.title: And people who can’t see the screen?
items.description: Every scene has a text equivalent: an index, a description, a list. Anyone who can’t see the 3D gets the same information.

items.title: Won’t it make people dizzy?
items.description: If your system asks for less motion, the experience stays still. Nobody should get dizzy looking at a catalogue.

items.question: Does it cover the European Accessibility Act?
items.answer: Yes. For websites, the technical reference is the European standard EN 301 549. Its new version, V4.1.1 (September 2026), moves from WCAG 2.1 to WCAG 2.2 AA, and that’s what I already audit against: once it is cited in the EU Official Journal it becomes the legal reference, and your report will already be up to date. The audit includes the compliance document ready to publish, written for your regime — in Spain, the information required by article 13.2 of Law 11/2023, or the formal accessibility statement of Royal Decree 1112/2018 for the public sector.

items.question: Will this improve my Google ranking?
items.answer: It’s not a ranking shortcut, and be wary of anyone who sells it that way. But much of what I fix is the same thing that helps Google understand your site: meaningful titles and headings, images with alt text, links that say where they go and pages that load fast. What improves things for a screen reader user usually improves them for a search engine too.

items.question: Will it change my website’s design?
items.answer: Rarely in a visible way. Most fixes live in the code: names, structure, focus order. When something visible has to change, like a colour without enough contrast or a button that’s too small, I show you first and we find the version that respects your brand.

agents.title: The same website, ready for AI too.
agents.text: AI assistants already search, compare and fill in forms on people’s behalf. Many don’t look at the screen: they read the accessibility tree, the same structure a screen reader uses. A button with no name is as invisible to them as it is to a blind person. So when I fix your website’s accessibility, I also make it ready for them.

meta.title: Real case: an in-depth accessibility audit | Javier Piedra
meta.description: A real public website audited in depth: all 50 criteria one by one, by hand and with a real screen reader. This is what I find and what you receive.

hero.subtitle: A real, anonymised case. I show you how I really audit — all 50 criteria one by one, by hand and with a screen reader — and what the client receives at the end. No names and no finger-pointing: the value is in the method.

contexto.title: A large tourism website with online booking
contexto.body1: The case is a large public website in the tourism sector, with online booking. By its nature, two frameworks apply at once: the public-sector one and, for the booking service sold to consumers, Spain’s Law 11/2023 (the transposition of the European Accessibility Act). The technical bar is the same in both: the EN 301 549 standard, which is equivalent to WCAG 2.1 AA.
contexto.body2: It’s the kind of website a scanner can’t cover: lots of pages, repeated templates and a booking process where the money is at stake. Exactly where a serious audit makes the difference.

metodo.title: It isn’t running a tool. It’s this.
metodo.intro: An automated test detects around 30% of the real problems. The rest can only be seen by hand. This is how I work on every audit:

steps.title: A representative sample
steps.text: You don’t audit the whole website (it isn’t feasible), but a sample that covers the home page, the booking process, forms, login and common templates. If a template fails, it fails on every page that uses it.

steps.title: All 50 criteria, one by one
steps.text: I evaluate the 50 level A and AA criteria of WCAG 2.1 on the sample, not just the ones a machine detects. Each with its status: passes, fails or not applicable.

steps.title: By hand and with a real screen reader
steps.text: Keyboard navigation, contrast, focus and reading with NVDA, the screen reader real people use. Automated tools can’t tell whether a field is announced properly; the screen reader can.

steps.title: Deliverables that prove the work
steps.text: A technical report, a conformance table for the 50 criteria, an accessibility statement ready to publish and, where relevant, a score in the style of Spain’s Web Accessibility Observatory.

hallazgos.title: Real failures, in plain language
hallazgos.intro: Some of the findings in this case, explained without jargon. None of them is rare: they come up in almost every website I audit.

items.title: A booking form without labels
items.text: Fields that are obvious to the eye, but that a screen reader announces as just a text box. Someone who can’t see doesn’t know what is being asked. In a booking, that’s a purchase that never gets completed.

items.title: The invisible focus
items.text: Navigating with the keyboard, you couldn’t see where you were: like moving around your house in the dark. It’s fixed with one line of CSS, but it affects the whole website.

items.title: The calendar the keyboard can’t reach
items.text: The date picker only responded to the mouse. Without a mouse, there was no way to book.

items.title: What the machine passed and the screen reader didn’t
items.text: A field the tool considered fine — it had a label — but that the real screen reader announced without a name, because that label was hidden with CSS. In theory, yes; for the user, no.

entregables.title: A report people can understand, that proves what was done
entregables.intro: Neither a 200-page PDF nor a tool dump. Clear, branded documents, written so management can understand them and your technical team can act on them.

items.title: Technical report
items.text: A verdict, findings by severity, the impact on people and a concrete fix, with code where it applies.

items.title: Conformance table for the 50 criteria
items.text: The status of every level A and AA criterion. Proof that everything has been reviewed, not just what jumps out.

items.title: Accessibility statement
items.text: Written for the regime that applies to you, ready to publish and meet the documentation requirement.

items.title: Results meeting
items.text: An hour to go through it with you and your team and set priorities. I don’t send you a PDF and disappear.

cierre.text: That’s exactly what I do: an in-depth audit, with a report and a compliance document tailored to your case. No smoke and no surprises.
